A spiral is a curve that winds around a central point or axis, progressively getting closer to or farther from the center. Spirals appear ubiquitously in nature and mathematics, from nautilus shells and galaxy arms to the solutions of differential equations in physics. The Archimedean spiral is the simplest type, with evenly-spaced turns. Its polar equation is r equals a theta, where a is a constant. The logarithmic spiral expands at a constant exponential rate and has the equation r equals a times e to the power of b theta. It appears in biology, from ammonite shells to hawk flight paths. The Fermat spiral or parabolic spiral has the equation r squared equals a squared theta, and its behavior is intermediate between the Archimedean and logarithmic types. A spiral is never closed—it passes through infinitely many points and cannot return to its starting location without crossing itself. The Golden Spiral, an approximation to the logarithmic spiral using Fibonacci rectangles, appears in art, design, and nature with surprising frequency. Spirals also appear in curl dynamics: water draining from a bath, tornadoes, and rotating astrophysical objects all form spiral patterns. Archimedes himself studied the spiral bearing his name and discovered its mathematical properties. His spiral was used in ancient Greek technology for pumping water and grinding grain.
